text: In Zeno's Achilles paradox, swift Achilles gives a tortoise a head start; each time he reaches where the tortoise was, it has crept a little farther on, so he seemingly can never catch it. What is the standard mathematical response to this paradox?
choices: Deny that space and time are infinitely divisible, treating them instead as built from discrete, indivisible units
The infinitely many 'catching-up' intervals form a convergent series whose total time is finite, so Achilles overtakes the tortoise in a finite time
Concede that Achilles literally never catches the tortoise, since motion itself is ultimately an illusion
Point out that at each instant Achilles occupies a space equal to himself and is therefore at rest
explanation: The standard mathematical response notes that the successive intervals (100/v, 10/v, 1/v, ...) form a convergent geometric series summing to a finite time, so Achilles catches the tortoise. Option 0 is a genuinely different, discrete-space strategy, not the convergence answer; option 2 simply accepts the Eleatic conclusion Zeno was defending; and option 3 confuses the Achilles with a different Zeno paradox, the Arrow.
